newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Released Moslem prisoners embittered at NATO.
newsitem.headline: Released Moslem prisoners embittered at NATO.

text.p: Four Moslem refugees released from a Serb prison after a controversial trial condemned U.S. peacekeeping troops on Friday for handing them over to their Bosnian Serb foes.
The men were sentenced to a year's imprisonment for illegal possession of weapons by a Bosnian Serb court on Thursday but were released because they had spent 12 months in pre-trial custody.
Three other Moslems arrested with them were sentenced to 20 years imprisonment for the alleged murder of Serb wood cutters.
U.N. officials criticised the trial because the men were denied lawyers of their own and were represented by Serb lawyers who were unfamiliar with the case.
The seven Moslems were refugees from the east Bosnian Moslem town of Srebrenica who surrendered to U.S. NATO troops last May.
They claimed to have been on the run since Bosnian Serb forces captured Srebrenica in July 1995 and allegedly massacred up to 4,000 Moslem men of fighting age.
"The (Americans) gave us to the Serbs even though we told them we were from Srebrenica," one of the released, Samir Avdic, said bitterly.
The group claimed they escaped Serb forces and hid in abandoned houses around Srebrenica until they surrendered in a U.S. camp near Serb town of Zvornik.

They were questioned and turned over to the Serb police because they were found in possession of some grenades and pistols, making them technically an armed group in violation of the Bosnian peace agreement.

Subsequent reports indicated the Moslems should have been kept in U.S. army custody until it could be established whether, as survivors of the Serb conquest of Srebrenica, they had violated the accord.
The group said they were among among a handful of survivors who hid near Srebrenica.
"We stayed in a cottage near the town, drank water from a creek and ploughed deserted garden plots for potatoes," Vahdet Avdic, 32, said.

They found a radio in an abandoned house which brought the news of Bosnia's peace accord signing in December 1995 but did not know how to reach the Moslem-Croat territory or how to cross the mined former frontlines.
In spring of 1996 the group decided to make a move towards the federation territory and sent three men to find a way but were unsucessful and the group started to wander around, Vahdet Avdic said.
They were spotted by U.S. peacekeepers while moving on foot in the forest.
"At first we were happy to see the American soldiers but we were disappointed pretty soon because a blue Serb police car showed up," Vahdet said.
"They either did not understand us or did not want to help us," another Moslem in the group, Muharem Hasanovic, said.
Emotions ran high with men who felt they were betrayed by NATO soldiers they put their trust in.

"The four of us are going to wait two weeks to see if the other three are released but if not, the first NATO soldiers we encounter, we'll take them and demand exchange for our guys," Samir Avdic threatened.
A NATO spokesman in Sarajevo said he hoped the reaction came from a man just released from a prison.
"But we do take every threat against the Stabilisation Forces seriously," Major Jan Joosten said.
